pages.title: Score exploitation & Pitfalls
pages.role: Create the need for guardrails and a constrained reward.
pages.core_message: A capable optimizer will exploit whatever the objective fails to measure.
talking_points: Score gains can come from keyword or structural manipulation.
The rewriter can invent unsupported guidance.
Cross-language semantic behavior can reward unwanted translation.
Mean improvement can conceal individual query damage.
Document my pitfall trajectory

- Before feeding the P1 contributing factors (page,h1,href/query semantic similarity; structural features etc.) the rewriter LLM only knows how to modify the editorial tone and rephrase certain sentence.

- Then it start gaming the scorer by translating certain portion of paragraphs into Japanese for boosting JP prompts P1 scores while not tanking on other prompts that much. Rewriting should not translate, thus inspire the language guardrail

- Then it started to modify important factoids to fit the prompt (e.g Service expand support to Germany when its not, hallucinating price deals) thus inspiring the fidelity check LLM guardrail (ask GPT5 to assess if rewrite twisted the factoids, raise concern whenever detected) -- this is the worst of all. For GEPA loop we even had to model fidelity violation as penalty so model wouldn't game on this
Check  Downloads/exploitation-proof-1.pdf to show the Japanese example.
pages.visual: A score increase paired with a clearly unacceptable content change.
questions: Which exploitation example had the strongest evidence?
Should this be framed as a red-team finding or expected optimizer behavior?
Which failure surprised you most during the trial?
answers: This is a good framing, imo, AEO is essentially a red/white team adversarial game, and red is incentivized to exploit, so we need to invest in leveling up white team or design arbiter rubrics otherwise the game's doomed to be lop-sided.
